lessons.title: Hybridization
lessons.idea: Count the domains around the atom, not the bonds: four domains is sp3, three is sp2, two is sp.

visual.caption: Same middle carbon, three jobs. Each bond counts once, single, double or triple, and each lone pair counts once. Water's oxygen makes two bonds but carries two lone pairs: four domains, sp3, bent.

steps: Pick the atom and count what is around it. Each bond is one domain.
Add one domain for each lone pair, even when nobody drew it.
Four is sp3 and 109.5 degrees, three is sp2 and 120, two is sp and 180.

connect.text: Orbital, the O in CARDIO: more s-character holds a pair closer to the nucleus. sp is 50 percent s, sp2 33, sp3 25, so an sp C-H (pKa about 25) is far more acidic than sp2 (about 44) or sp3 (about 50). That is why NaNH2 can pull the proton off a terminal alkyne in Unit 8. And a flat sp2 carbocation is why SN1 comes out racemic in Unit 7.

traps.example: Here: a double bond is one domain, not two, and a lone pair counts too. Water's oxygen is sp3 even with only two bonds.
traps.name: Hybridization or s-character misread
traps.fix: Count electron domains (4 is sp3, 3 is sp2, 2 is sp); more s-character holds an anion closer, so sp C-H (pKa about 25) beats sp2 and sp3.

traps.example: Here: an atom with a lone pair next to a pi bond can be sp2, because the pair joins the pi system (the N of an amide).
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: count lone pairs from the formal charge before you count domains; a minus adds a pair.
traps.name: Arrow or formal charge bookkeeping slip
traps.fix: Arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point where the electrons go; recount formal charge (valence minus dots minus sticks) on every atom an arrow touches.

lessons.title: Formal charge
lessons.idea: Formal charge is bookkeeping: what the atom brought minus what it is holding, where a lone pair counts two and a bond counts one.

visual.caption: One oxygen, three charges. Oxygen always brings six. Holding: two for each lone pair, one for each bond. Brought minus holding is the charge.

steps: Write what the atom brought: carbon 4, nitrogen 5, oxygen 6.
Count what it holds: two per lone pair, one per bond.
Brought minus holding is the formal charge.

connect.text: Charge, the C in CARDIO, starts here: a positive acid like CH3OH2+ is far stronger than a neutral one. You need formal charge to check every curved arrow (Unit 1) and every resonance form, and the minus on methoxide is what makes it a strong base and a good nucleophile in Unit 6.

traps.example: Here: a bond counts one electron for the atom, a lone pair counts two. In CH3OH2+ the plus sits on oxygen even though oxygen is the most electronegative atom.
traps.name: Arrow or formal charge bookkeeping slip
traps.fix: Arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point where the electrons go; recount formal charge (valence minus dots minus sticks) on every atom an arrow touches.

traps.example: Here: a neutral molecule can still carry a plus and a minus. Trimethylamine N-oxide, (CH3)3N-O, has N+ and O-.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: formal charge comes from the count, not from which atom pulls harder.
traps.name: Atom size vs electronegativity mixed up
traps.fix: Down a column, size wins (HI is a stronger acid than HF); across a row, electronegativity wins (HF beats H2O beats NH3).

lessons.title: Resonance structures
lessons.idea: Resonance spreads a charge over more atoms by moving only pi electrons and lone pairs, and every atom that shares the charge makes it more stable.

visual.caption: Acetate. A lone pair on the negative oxygen makes a new pi bond while the old pi bond moves onto the other oxygen. No atom moves and no single bond breaks. The real ion is the average: about minus one half on each oxygen.

steps: Find the pi bond or lone pair next to the charge. Only those move.
Push one step: lone pair into a bond, or pi bond onto the neighbor atom.
Count the atoms that end up sharing the charge. More helpers, more stable.

connect.text: Resonance, the R in CARDIO: acetate shares its charge over two oxygens, so acetic acid (pKa 4.8) beats ethanol (16) in Unit 2. The same spreading makes allylic and benzylic cations stable (Unit 6), steers EAS (Unit 11) and makes the alpha-H acidic (Unit 14).

traps.example: Here: acetate never sits as one form; both oxygens are the same all the time, and the real ion is the average.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: if your arrow moved a hydrogen or broke a single bond, that is a different molecule, not a resonance form.
traps.name: Arrow or formal charge bookkeeping slip
traps.fix: Arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point where the electrons go; recount formal charge (valence minus dots minus sticks) on every atom an arrow touches.

traps.example: Here: resonance cannot pass through an sp3 carbon, because it has no p orbital to share.
traps.name: Hybridization or s-character misread
traps.fix: Count electron domains (4 is sp3, 3 is sp2, 2 is sp); more s-character holds an anion closer, so sp C-H (pKa about 25) beats sp2 and sp3.

lessons.title: Conjugation
lessons.idea: Conjugated means the p orbitals sit side by side with no sp3 carbon between them, so electrons and charge can spread along the whole run.

visual.caption: Top: hexa-1,3-diene, four p orbitals in a row, one conjugated system. Bottom: hexa-1,5-diene, two sp3 carbons break the row into two isolated pi bonds.

steps: Mark every sp2 or sp atom with a p orbital.
Look for an unbroken row of them. One sp3 carbon breaks the row.
An unbroken row, or a charge right next to a pi bond, is conjugated.

connect.text: Conjugation is resonance with room to run. A charge next to a pi bond is allylic, next to a ring is benzylic, and either one jumps up the cation and radical stability ladders (Units 6 and 10). Diels-Alder needs a conjugated diene (Unit 10), and an enone is attacked at the beta carbon in Michael addition (Unit 14).

traps.example: Here: two pi bonds with an sp3 carbon between them are isolated, not conjugated.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: mark each atom sp2, sp or sp3 first; one sp3 carbon breaks the row of p orbitals.
traps.name: Hybridization or s-character misread
traps.fix: Count electron domains (4 is sp3, 3 is sp2, 2 is sp); more s-character holds an anion closer, so sp C-H (pKa about 25) beats sp2 and sp3.

traps.example: Here: a ring alone means nothing. Cyclohexene is a ring with one pi bond; count p orbitals in a row.
traps.name: Aromaticity misjudged (Huckel count, lone pair in or out)
traps.fix: Aromatic needs cyclic, planar, fully conjugated and 4n+2 pi electrons; count a lone pair only if that atom has no pi bond already in the ring.

lessons.title: Polarity and dipole moments
lessons.idea: Each polar bond points toward the more electronegative atom, and the molecule is polar only if those bond dipoles do not cancel in 3D.

visual.caption: Acetone: one C=O dipole, nothing to cancel it, net dipole. Carbon dioxide: two C=O dipoles on a straight line pointing opposite ways, net zero.

steps: Find the bully: the more electronegative atom gets the partial minus.
Draw each bond dipole toward it.
Add them in 3D. Equal and opposite cancel; anything left over is the net dipole.

connect.text: Dipole, the D in CARDIO: a polar bond next to a charge pulls density, which is induction. The partial plus carbon of C=O is the target for every nucleophile in Units 12 and 13, and polarity sets boiling point, solubility and TLC Rf in Units 3 and 5.

traps.example: Here: a long carbon tail can outweigh one OH or C=O, so one polar group does not make a molecule water soluble.
traps.name: Polarity or IMF trend flipped (boiling point, solubility, dipole)
traps.fix: Rank by intermolecular forces (H-bond > dipole > London), then by surface area: more H-bonding and more surface raise boiling point, and like dissolves like.

traps.example: Here: CO2 and CCl4 have polar bonds but no net dipole, because the bond dipoles cancel. CH2Cl2 does not cancel in 3D.
traps.name: Missed the symmetry (equivalent H or C)
traps.fix: Draw the mirror plane or rotation axis first; atoms that swap places under it give one signal.

traps.example: Here: the dipole points to the more electronegative atom: F, then O, then Cl and N.
traps.name: Atom size vs electronegativity mixed up
traps.fix: Down a column, size wins (HI is a stronger acid than HF); across a row, electronegativity wins (HF beats H2O beats NH3).

lessons.title: Arrow-pushing
lessons.idea: A curved arrow starts at electrons and ends where they go: a full head moves a pair, a fishhook moves one electron.

visual.caption: Top: hydroxide's lone pair attacks the carbon, and the C-Br bond leaves with Br. Two full-headed arrows, two electrons each. Bottom: light splits Br2 evenly. Two fishhooks, one electron each, two radicals.

steps: Find the electrons: a lone pair, a pi bond or a minus. The arrow starts there.
Find the poor atom: a partial plus carbon or an acidic H. The arrow ends there.
If that atom already has four bonds, a second arrow kicks one bond onto the leaving group.

connect.text: The ADA asks it both ways: predict the product from the arrows, and draw the arrows from the product. Every mechanism unit uses this one move. The first ADA single mechanism, proton transfer, is the same arrows on a hydrogen (Unit 2), and fishhooks come back in radical halogenation (Unit 10).

traps.example: Here: an arrow never starts at a positive charge or at an atom, and a fishhook moves only one electron.
traps.name: Arrow or formal charge bookkeeping slip
traps.fix: Arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point where the electrons go; recount formal charge (valence minus dots minus sticks) on every atom an arrow touches.

traps.example: Here: a carbon with four bonds cannot take a fifth. When the nucleophile attacks, draw the bond to the leaving group breaking in the same step.
traps.name: Steps out of order or a step skipped (synthesis or mechanism)
traps.fix: Work backward from the target one bond at a time, and check that each step leaves a group the next reagent can use (directors, protecting groups, oxidation level).

traps.example: Here: light splitting Br2 is radical, so fishhooks; hydroxide attacking carbon is polar, so full heads.
traps.name: Radical vs ionic pathway mixed up (peroxide, NBS, light)
traps.fix: Light, heat or peroxide means radicals: HBr with ROOR adds anti-Markovnikov (HBr only), and NBS substitutes the allylic or benzylic H instead of adding.

lessons.title: Bronsted-Lowry acids and bases
lessons.idea: An acid gives a proton and a base takes it, and the equilibrium always lies on the side of the weaker acid.

visual.caption: Acetic acid gives its proton to hydroxide. Two arrows: the lone pair takes the H, and the O-H bond stays behind on acetate. Acetic acid (pKa 4.8) is a far stronger acid than water (15.7), so the right side wins.

steps: Find the H that moves. The one that loses it is the acid; its leftover is the conjugate base.
The one that gains it is the base; it becomes the conjugate acid.
Compare the two acids by pKa. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid, the higher pKa.

connect.text: This is GChem acid-base with skeletal drawings. It is also the first ADA single mechanism: a proton transfer drawn with two curved arrows. Every CARDIO ranking in this unit answers one question: which side of an equation like this one wins.

traps.example: Here: acetic acid (4.8) gives its proton to hydroxide because water (15.7) is the weaker acid.
traps.name: Acid-base direction or strength reversed (pKa, equilibrium, base strength)
traps.fix: Lower pKa is the stronger acid, and an acid-base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base (the higher pKa).

traps.example: Here: acetate is the conjugate base of acetic acid, not of water. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H+.
traps.name: Judged the acid instead of its conjugate base
traps.fix: To compare acids, remove the H and ask which anion is more stable; the more stable conjugate base belongs to the stronger acid.

traps.example: Here: the base's lone pair attacks the H. The arrow starts at the base's electrons, never at the proton.
traps.name: Arrow or formal charge bookkeeping slip
traps.fix: Arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point where the electrons go; recount formal charge (valence minus dots minus sticks) on every atom an arrow touches.

lessons.title: pKa and relative acidity
lessons.idea: Lower pKa means a stronger acid, and a base can fully deprotonate any acid with a lower pKa than its own conjugate acid.

visual.caption: The anchors. When two compounds sit in different anchor groups, the anchors answer the question before CARDIO does.

steps: Place each acid on the anchor line.
Lower pKa, stronger acid. Each pKa unit is a factor of 10.
A base works on any acid below its own conjugate acid. NaNH2 (NH3, 38) takes the H off a terminal alkyne (25); NaOH (water, 15.7) cannot.

connect.text: The line is CARDIO in numbers: acids (4 to 5) beat alcohols (16 to 18) by Resonance, and alkyne (25) beats alkene (44) by Orbital. Unit 5 uses it to pick the extraction layer, and Unit 14 uses it for enolates: a 1,3-dicarbonyl sits near pKa 9, a plain ketone near 19 to 20.

traps.example: Here: pKa 4.8 is a stronger acid than pKa 16, and NaOH (water, 15.7) cannot fully deprotonate a terminal alkyne (25).
traps.name: Acid-base direction or strength reversed (pKa, equilibrium, base strength)
traps.fix: Lower pKa is the stronger acid, and an acid-base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base (the higher pKa).

traps.example: Here: carboxylic acids (4 to 5) beat alcohols (16 to 18) because the carboxylate shares its charge over two oxygens.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: a nearby halogen lowers the pKa; an alkyl group nudges it up.
traps.name: Induction misjudged (distance, or donor vs withdrawer)
traps.fix: Electron-withdrawing groups (halogens, NO2, C=O) stabilize anions and raise acidity, more strongly the closer they sit; alkyl groups donate and do the opposite.

lessons.title: Conjugate base stability
lessons.idea: Judge the conjugate base: the more stable the base an acid leaves behind, the stronger the acid.

visual.caption: Ethoxide holds its minus on one oxygen. Acetate shares it over two. Charge, Atom tie (both minus, both on O), so Resonance decides: acetic acid (4.8) is far stronger than ethanol (16).

steps: Take the acidic H off both acids. Now compare the two bases.
Walk C, A, R, D and I, O in order: Charge, Atom, Resonance, Dipole and Induction, Orbital.
Stop at the first letter that differs. That letter decides.

connect.text: The happy base comes back everywhere. A stable anion is a weak base and a good leaving group (I- beats Br- beats Cl-, Unit 6), and the carbonyl ladder ranks acid derivatives by how stable their leaving group is (Unit 13).

traps.example: Here: acetate shares its minus over two oxygens; ethoxide holds it on one. Resonance decides once Charge and Atom tie.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: the proton is the same H+ every time, so strip it and compare the two bases.
traps.name: Judged the acid instead of its conjugate base
traps.fix: To compare acids, remove the H and ask which anion is more stable; the more stable conjugate base belongs to the stronger acid.

traps.example: Here: the more stable base belongs to the stronger acid, which has the lower pKa.
traps.name: Acid-base direction or strength reversed (pKa, equilibrium, base strength)
traps.fix: Lower pKa is the stronger acid, and an acid-base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base (the higher pKa).

lessons.title: Inductive and resonance effects on acidity
lessons.idea: An electron-withdrawing group near the charge pulls density through the bonds and stabilizes the conjugate base, and the pull fades fast with distance.

visual.caption: Propanoic acid, then a chlorine on carbon 3, then on carbon 2, right next to the COOH. The closer the chlorine, the stronger the acid. pKa values are standard reference values, rounded.

steps: Find the electron-withdrawing atom and the charge on the conjugate base.
Count the bonds between them. Close is a strong pull, a few bonds away is almost nothing.
More pullers and more electronegative pullers pull harder: F beats Cl beats Br beats I.

connect.text: One idea, three units: an electron-withdrawing group raises acidity here, is meta-directing and deactivating in EAS (Unit 11), and makes an acyl carbon more reactive (Unit 13). A para nitro group pulls by resonance as well as induction, which is why it makes a phenol more acidic.

traps.example: Here: chlorine on carbon 2 (pKa about 2.8) pulls far harder than on carbon 3 (about 4.0); a few bonds farther and it barely counts.
traps.name: Induction misjudged (distance, or donor vs withdrawer)
traps.fix: Electron-withdrawing groups (halogens, NO2, C=O) stabilize anions and raise acidity, more strongly the closer they sit; alkyl groups donate and do the opposite.

traps.example: Here: F pulls harder than Cl, which pulls harder than Br; for induction, electronegativity is what counts.
traps.name: Atom size vs electronegativity mixed up
traps.fix: Down a column, size wins (HI is a stronger acid than HF); across a row, electronegativity wins (HF beats H2O beats NH3).

traps.example: Here: a para nitro group pulls by resonance too, which does not fade along the ring the way induction does.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

lessons.title: Amine basicity
lessons.idea: An amine is basic when its lone pair is free to grab a proton; tie that pair up in resonance and the base gets weaker.

visual.caption: Methylamine's lone pair is free. Aniline's lone pair spreads into the ring, and an amide's spreads onto the carbonyl oxygen. Numbers are the pKa of each conjugate acid; the amide value is approximate.

steps: Find the nitrogen's lone pair.
Is it next to a pi bond or ring? If yes, it is in resonance and less available.
More available pair, stronger base, higher conjugate-acid pKa.

connect.text: Lone-pair donors push density: the same NH2 that is a weak base in aniline makes the ring an ortho/para activator in EAS (Unit 11). And an amide's tied-up nitrogen is why amides sit at the bottom of the carbonyl ladder (Unit 13).

traps.example: Here: a strong base has a high conjugate-acid pKa. Methylamine (10.6) is a stronger base than aniline (4.6).
traps.name: Acid-base direction or strength reversed (pKa, equilibrium, base strength)
traps.fix: Lower pKa is the stronger acid, and an acid-base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base (the higher pKa).

traps.example: Here: aniline's lone pair spreads into the ring and an amide's onto the C=O, so both are weak bases. Pyrrole's pair is part of its aromatic sextet.
traps.name: Missed (or overrated) the resonance
traps.fix: Look for a lone pair, pi bond or charge next to a pi bond; delocalized charge is stabilized, and a lone pair tied up in resonance is less basic and less nucleophilic.

traps.example: Here: alkyl groups donate and raise basicity a little; a CF3 group nearby withdraws and lowers it a lot.
traps.name: Induction misjudged (distance, or donor vs withdrawer)
traps.fix: Electron-withdrawing groups (halogens, NO2, C=O) stabilize anions and raise acidity, more strongly the closer they sit; alkyl groups donate and do the opposite.

lessons.title: Intermolecular forces
lessons.idea: Molecules hold each other by the strongest force they can make: hydrogen bonds beat dipole-dipole, which beats London dispersion.

visual.caption: Methanol: an O-H on one molecule reaches a lone pair on the next, a hydrogen bond. Acetone: the partial plus carbon of one C=O lines up with the partial minus oxygen of the next. Propane: only London forces, which every molecule has.

steps: H-bond donor: H on N, O or F. Acceptor: a lone pair on N, O or F.
No donor but a net dipole: dipole-dipole.
Everything has London forces, and they grow with surface area and size.

connect.text: This is GChem liquids and solids. Ethanol and dimethyl ether share the formula C2H6O, but ethanol boils at 78 C and the ether at -24 C: one O-H makes the difference. The same forces decide solubility, TLC Rf and which layer a compound sits in during extraction (Unit 5), and protic vs aprotic solvent (Unit 7).

traps.example: Here: acetone accepts H-bonds but has no O-H to give, so pure acetone has no hydrogen bonding. Butan-1-ol and diethyl ether weigh the same (74 g/mol), yet the alcohol boils about 80 degrees higher.
traps.name: Polarity or IMF trend flipped (boiling point, solubility, dipole)
traps.fix: Rank by intermolecular forces (H-bond > dipole > London), then by surface area: more H-bonding and more surface raise boiling point, and like dissolves like.

traps.example: Here: find the H on N, O or F first. An ether O or a ketone O is an acceptor only.
traps.name: Functional group misidentified (ester vs ketone vs aldehyde vs acid vs amide)
traps.fix: Name what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon (H aldehyde, two C ketone, OH acid, OR ester, N amide) before using any rule that depends on the group.

traps.example: Here: the same forces set TLC Rf and which layer a compound sits in during extraction (Unit 5).
traps.name: Lab technique step misjudged (TLC, extraction, recrystallization, distillation)
traps.fix: Tie each step to one property: TLC and columns separate by polarity, extraction by charge (pKa vs the layer pH), recrystallization by hot-vs-cold solubility, distillation by boiling point.

lessons.title: Boiling point and solubility trends
lessons.idea: Same forces, more contact, higher boiling point: branching makes a molecule rounder, cuts its surface contact and lowers its boiling point.

visual.caption: Three C5H12 isomers, the same mass and the same force (London only). The straight chain touches its neighbors the most and boils highest. Boiling points are standard values.

steps: Rank by the strongest IMF first: H-bonding, then dipole, then London.
Same IMF type: bigger molecule, higher boiling point.
Same formula: more branching, lower boiling point.

connect.text: Boiling point order is what comes over first in distillation (Unit 5), and polarity is what moves on silica in TLC. Melting point is different: a compact, symmetric molecule packs well, so branching can raise a melting point even as it lowers the boiling point.

traps.example: Here: for isomers with the same forces, branching lowers the boiling point: pentane 36 C, 2,2-dimethylpropane 10 C.
traps.name: Polarity or IMF trend flipped (boiling point, solubility, dipole)
traps.fix: Rank by intermolecular forces (H-bond > dipole > London), then by surface area: more H-bonding and more surface raise boiling point, and like dissolves like.

traps.example: Here: on silica TLC the nonpolar compound travels farther and has the higher Rf; in distillation the lower boiling compound comes over first.
traps.name: Lab technique step misjudged (TLC, extraction, recrystallization, distillation)
traps.fix: Tie each step to one property: TLC and columns separate by polarity, extraction by charge (pKa vs the layer pH), recrystallization by hot-vs-cold solubility, distillation by boiling point.

traps.example: Here: an acid moves into a basic water layer only if the base is strong enough to deprotonate it; compare the pKa values.
traps.name: Acid-base direction or strength reversed (pKa, equilibrium, base strength)
traps.fix: Lower pKa is the stronger acid, and an acid-base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base (the higher pKa).

lessons.title: Degrees of unsaturation (IHD)
lessons.idea: Each ring or pi bond is one degree of unsaturation: look and count when you have a drawing, use the formula only when you have just a molecular formula.

visual.caption: C6H10 has IHD 2. Three ways to spend it: one ring and one pi bond, two pi bonds, or one triple bond (two pi bonds). Every drawing here is checked to be C6H10.

steps: Drawing in front of you: rings plus pi bonds. A triple bond is two.
Formula only: IHD = (2C + 2 + N - H - X) / 2. Ignore oxygen.
IHD 4 or more with six carbons: think benzene ring first.

connect.text: IHD is the first move in every structure-from-spectra item (Unit 5): the formula tells you how many rings and pi bonds to look for before IR and NMR place them. A benzene ring is 4 by itself, which also matters for aromaticity counts in Unit 11.

traps.example: Here: in the formula a halogen counts like an H, a nitrogen adds one, and oxygen changes nothing.
traps.name: Spectroscopy landmark misread (IR band, NMR shift, splitting, integration)
traps.fix: Anchor on the landmarks first (IR 1700 C=O, broad 3300 O-H, 2200 triple bond; NMR 9-10 aldehyde, 10-12 acid, 6.5-8 aromatic), then use n+1 splitting and integration.

traps.example: Here: the bracket counts missing hydrogens; each degree is two missing H, so divide by two.
traps.name: Arithmetic or ratio inverted (ee, rotation, pKa ratio)
traps.fix: Write the formula before the numbers: ee = (major - minor) / total x 100, observed rotation = ee x specific rotation, and each pKa unit is a factor of 10.

traps.example: Here: a benzene ring is four degrees, one ring plus three double bonds, whether drawn with lines or a circle.
traps.name: Product bookkeeping slip: carbon count, ring size, or how many times it reacts
traps.fix: Count carbons and rings in the start, the carbon-adding reagents and the product, and read the equivalents: excess reagent hits every reactive site, one equivalent hits the most reactive one.

lessons.title: Alkane and functional group naming
lessons.idea: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical prefixes: number from the end that hits a branch first.

visual.caption: The same six-carbon chain numbered both ways. From the right the branches land on 2 and 4; from the left, 3 and 5. The first point of difference picks 2,4: 2,4-dimethylhexane.

steps: Find the longest continuous chain. It may turn a corner. Count it: that is the base name.
Number from the end that gives the first branch the lowest number.
Name the branches as prefixes in alphabetical order, then add the suffix.

connect.text: Every product question is read through the name in the stem and the choices. Counting carbons carefully also keeps you safe in synthesis (Unit 15), where a step that adds or removes a carbon changes the base name.

traps.example: Here: the longest chain can turn a corner, and you keep the locant set that is lower at the first difference (2,4 beats 3,5).
traps.name: Naming slip: wrong chain, numbering or suffix
traps.fix: Find the longest chain that holds the highest-priority group, number from the end that gives it the lowest locant, then list substituents alphabetically.

traps.example: Here: prefixes go in alphabetical order (ethyl before methyl); di, tri and tetra do not count for the alphabet.
traps.name: R/S or E/Z priority slip
traps.fix: Rank by atomic number at the first point of difference, and if the lowest priority points at you, reverse the direction you read.

traps.example: Here: name the group on the chain before you pick the suffix: ol, al, one, oic acid.
traps.name: Functional group misidentified (ester vs ketone vs aldehyde vs acid vs amide)
traps.fix: Name what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon (H aldehyde, two C ketone, OH acid, OR ester, N amide) before using any rule that depends on the group.

lessons.title: Functional group priority
lessons.idea: The highest-priority group gets the suffix and the lowest number; every other group becomes a prefix.

visual.caption: The suffix ladder, highest at the top. Below: a ketone outranks an alcohol, so the name ends in -one and the OH becomes hydroxy: 4-hydroxybutan-2-one.

steps: Find every functional group.
The one highest on the ladder takes the suffix and the lowest locant.
The rest become prefixes (hydroxy, oxo, amino). Halo, nitro and alkyl groups are always prefixes.

connect.text: Do not mix this ladder up with the carbonyl reactivity ladder in Unit 13. There, acid chlorides are the most reactive; here, a carboxylic acid outranks an acid chloride for the suffix. The two ladders answer different questions. Naming the group also tells you which IR landmark to look for in Unit 5.

traps.example: Here: with a ketone and an alcohol, the ketone takes the suffix and the lowest number; the OH becomes hydroxy: 4-hydroxybutan-2-one.
traps.name: Naming slip: wrong chain, numbering or suffix
traps.fix: Find the longest chain that holds the highest-priority group, number from the end that gives it the lowest locant, then list substituents alphabetically.

traps.example: Here: chloro, bromo, nitro and alkyl are always prefixes; they never take the suffix.
traps.name: Functional group misidentified (ester vs ketone vs aldehyde vs acid vs amide)
traps.fix: Name what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon (H aldehyde, two C ketone, OH acid, OR ester, N amide) before using any rule that depends on the group.

traps.example: Here: the naming ladder is not the reactivity ladder. An acid chloride is the most reactive acyl group, but a carboxylic acid outranks it for the suffix.
traps.name: Climbed the carbonyl ladder (acid derivative reactivity order)
traps.fix: Acyl substitution only goes downhill: acid chloride > anhydride > ester (acid) > amide, ranked by how weak a base the leaving group is.
